title: The Beatitudes and the Fulfillment of the Law
summary: Jesus goes up on a mountain and begins his first great discourse, the Sermon on the Mount, by pronouncing blessed the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. He calls his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them. In six contrasts (you have heard that it was said, but I tell you) he teaches a righteousness that reaches the heart, on anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love of enemies, ending with the call to be perfect as the Father is perfect.
story: Chapter 4 ended with crowds streaming to Jesus from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. Now he sits down on a mountain to teach, as a rabbi did, and his disciples gather close while the crowds listen (7:28). Readers who know Israel's story will think of Moses bringing God's law down from Mount Sinai. Jesus, who has just relived Israel's exodus and wilderness testing, now gives the charter of life in the kingdom he has been announcing. Chapters 5 to 7 are the first of Matthew's five discourses, and this chapter lays the foundation: who is blessed in God's kingdom, what the disciples are for, and how Jesus relates to the law of Moses.
historical:
The sermon is set in Galilee in the early part of Jesus' ministry, around AD 28 to 30. Tradition places it on a hill above the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee near Capernaum, where a church, the Church of the Beatitudes, now stands; the exact site is unknown. Luke records a shorter, similar sermon given on a level place (Luke 6:17-49). Many scholars think Matthew and Luke drew on a common body of teaching and that each arranged it for his purpose; others think Jesus, like any traveling teacher, gave similar teaching many times.

The antitheses engage live debates of the time. Jewish teachers argued over how to apply the law, and on divorce the schools associated with the teachers Hillel and Shammai, both of the generation before Jesus, disputed the meaning of some indecency in Deuteronomy 24:1. According to the Mishnah, the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for sexual unfaithfulness, while the school of Hillel allowed it for almost any cause. The command to hate one's enemy (verse 43) is not found in the Old Testament, but it reflected a common attitude, and the Community Rule found among the Dead Sea Scrolls instructs its members to hate the sons of darkness. Galilee was under Roman rule through Herod Antipas, and Roman soldiers could legally force civilians to carry their gear for a set distance, which lies behind verse 41.
cultural:
The word blessed in the Beatitudes was a familiar form of speech in Judaism, as in Psalm 1 and Psalm 32, pronouncing someone fortunate or favored by God. Jesus pronounces blessed exactly the people his culture would have pitied. The Old Testament often calls the poor, the humble, and the oppressed God's own people (Isaiah 61:1-3; Psalm 37:11, which says the meek will inherit the land), and the Beatitudes echo that language.

Several details reflect daily life. Salt was used to preserve and flavor food; the salt of the Dead Sea region, mixed with other minerals, could lose its taste. Oil lamps were small clay vessels placed on a stand to light a one-room house. A jot is the yodh, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and a stroke is a tiny mark distinguishing one letter from another. Raca was an Aramaic insult meaning something like empty-head. The Sanhedrin was the Jewish high council in Jerusalem. Hell translates Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had once been sacrificed to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31), which became a picture of final judgment. A slap on the right cheek, given by a right-handed person, was a backhanded insult, not a blow in a fight. The tunic was the inner garment and the cloak the outer one, which the law said a poor man could keep overnight even when pledged as security (Exodus 22:26-27).
literary: The chapter has three parts. The Beatitudes (verses 3 to 12) form a carefully balanced unit of eight blessings, the first and eighth ending with the same promise, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven, followed by a ninth blessing addressed directly to the disciples. The second part (verses 13 to 20) uses the images of salt and light and then states Jesus' thesis about the law (verses 17 to 20). The third part (verses 21 to 48) is six antitheses, each beginning with some form of you have heard that it was said and continuing but I tell you. Most quote or summarize the law of Moses (the Ten Commandments in the first two, Deuteronomy 24:1 in the third, Exodus 21:24 in the fifth); the last quotes Leviticus 19:18 alongside a popular addition. The chapter closes with a summary call, be perfect, which echoes Leviticus 19:2, you shall be holy, for I am holy, and frames all six contrasts.

outline.t: Jesus sits on the mountain to teach
Salt of the earth and light of the world
Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets

doctrines.note: The Beatitudes describe the people of the kingdom and promise them its gifts: comfort, the earth, mercy, the sight of God. The kingdom reverses the world's judgments about who is fortunate.

Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets rather than abolishing them. He interprets them with authority, drawing out their intent (the heart behind the act) and bringing them to their goal in his own teaching and work.
The call to be perfect as the Father is perfect echoes Leviticus: God's people are to reflect his character, above all his indiscriminate generosity to the evil and the good.

words.note: Makarios, blessed, fortunate, or happy in the sense of being well off before God. It is a declaration, not a command: Jesus does not tell people to become poor in spirit in order to earn blessing but announces that those who are so are favored in God's kingdom.

Pleroo, to fill or fulfill. Matthew uses it for prophecy coming true (1:22; 2:15), and in verse 17 for what Jesus does with the Law and the Prophets. Interpreters debate whether it means that Jesus obeys the law perfectly, interprets it rightly, or brings it to its intended goal; many think all three are included.

Geenna, Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom. Once a site of child sacrifice and later a symbol of God's judgment on the wicked, it became the common Jewish term for the place of final punishment. Jesus uses it more than anyone else in the New Testament.

Teleios, perfect, complete, mature, or whole. In verse 48 it does not mean flawless performance so much as wholeness and undivided love, a love that does not stop at friends. Luke's parallel says be merciful as your Father is merciful (Luke 6:36).

christ: The chapter reveals Jesus' authority. Moses delivered the law as God's word; Jesus says I tell you, placing his own word alongside and interpreting the law given at Sinai. He says blessed are those persecuted because of Me, assuming a loyalty to himself that the prophets reserved for God. He claims to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, and the rest of Matthew shows how: by his teaching, his perfect obedience, and his death, which he describes as the pouring out of his blood of the covenant (26:28). The Beatitudes are also a portrait of Jesus himself, the one who is meek and lowly (11:29), who shows mercy, makes peace, and is persecuted for righteousness, and who loves and prays for his enemies even from the cross (Luke 23:34). The disciples are called to live this way because they belong to him.

hard.q: Are Jesus' commands in this chapter meant to be kept literally, and are they for everyone?
hard.a:
Christians have read the Sermon on the Mount in several ways. The medieval church often distinguished commands binding on all believers from counsels of perfection for those in religious orders. Martin Luther and many Lutherans stressed that the sermon's demands expose our inability and drive us to grace, while also guiding believers in their personal lives, as distinct from their duties in public office. The Anabaptist tradition, including Mennonites, takes the commands directly: no oaths, no violence, and love of enemies as the normal path of discipleship. Albert Schweitzer argued that it was an interim ethic for a short time before an expected end, and older dispensational teachers applied it chiefly to a future kingdom. Most Christians today read it as the pattern of life for every disciple now, enabled by grace, with its sayings often using vivid overstatement (as in gouging out an eye) to show how seriously sin must be treated.

On specific commands, Christians differ. On divorce, some hold that sexual unfaithfulness permits divorce and remarriage, while others limit the exception to unfaithfulness during betrothal or to unlawful unions. On oaths, some refuse all oaths while others think Jesus forbids the evasive swearing of his day, not solemn oaths in court. On nonviolence, some hold that verses 38 to 42 forbid all use of force, while others read them as forbidding personal revenge but not the state's use of the sword to protect the innocent (Romans 13:4). All agree that Jesus calls his followers to a righteousness of the heart that exceeds outward rule keeping.

questions: Which of the Beatitudes most contradicts what your culture calls a good life, and which one do you most resist?
Jesus traces murder back to anger and adultery back to the look. Where in your life is he asking you to deal with the root rather than the fruit?
Love for enemies is the climax of the chapter. Who is the enemy you find hardest to pray for, and what would it mean to pray for them this week?
